Literature:
Christian Zervos, Pablo Picasso, Éditions Cahiers d'Art, Paris, 1932-1978, Vol. 31, no. 109 & 110, p. 36 (both illustrated).

Note:
In early 1969, late in his life and career, Pablo Picasso embarked on a series of paintings he called Portraits Imaginaires, or Imaginary Portraits, bursts of color and playfulness that referred to favorite subjects found in paintings by Rembrandt, or in literary classics by William Shakespeare, Honoré de Balzac, or Alexandre Dumas. Painted quickly on discarded pieces of corrugated cardboard that accompanied an art supply shipment, the works were theatrical, whimsical and bright, and later adapted into a suite of twenty-nine lithographs by the printmaker Marcel Salinas. Created between 1969 and 1972, the suite was published posthumously in 1973 by Salinas.

The present double-sided drawing, Tête d’Homme (with Deux Têtes verso), dates from this period. Executed in March 1969, it recalls Rembrandt’s seventeenth-century Dutch dandies while evoking Alexandre Dumas’ Three Musketeers, all attired in Louis XIII garments. With their swirling hair, beards, and playful gazes, these figures offer a stylized, fantastical guise for Picasso’s late-career reimaginings of a familiar and nostalgic theme. For the artist, the Musketeers embodied masculinity, vitality, power, and strength—and have even been described by art historians as his “alter ego,” a notion made all the more poignant by the fact that Picasso's health appeared to slightly decline at the time this drawing was created, the artist recovering from an invasive stomach surgery a few years prior.

Literature:

Ben Whitworth, The Sculpture of Leon Underwood, The Henry Moore Foundation in association with Lund Humphries, Much Hadham & Aldershot, 2000, no. 90, pp. 12-13; 38-39; 63; 130 (another cast illustrated).

Note:
Born in Shepherd’s Bush, London in 1890, Leon Underwood was a sculptor, painter, and teacher whose artistic impact has been appreciated more posthumously than during his lifetime. Underwood was a curious traveler, scholar and collector of non-Western art, deeply interested in African, Mexican, and Native American traditions, which he studied first-hand during his extensive travels. His 1934 publication Art for Heaven’s Sake was among the earliest English-language studies to champion African art as part of a sophisticated and spiritual tradition, rather than purely ethnographic artifact.

In African art in particular, Underwood understood a visual language which he could incorporate into his own work, to convey the dynamism and fluidity he desired in his forms. While teaching at the school he founded - Brook Green School of Art in London - Underwood would ask life models to change position frequently so that he and his students could learn to represent the balance, rhythm and vitality of the human body in motion. 

Of the present sculpture Negro Rhythm: Harlem, NY, in particular, artist and writer Christopher Neve mused: the work is "altogether more of an inspired scribble in the air, the patinated bronze as compulsive as a 12-bar chorus from New Orleans with its insistent syncopated beat, and even, round the base, its title in a rhythmic 1930s script- the whole object, twenty-two inches high, an inspired exercise as vividly period as Edith Sitwell’s 'allegro negro cocktail shaker.'" The lyrical nature of the dancer, throwing his head back and swirling around a central axis, brings the dynamic figure to life and encapsulates Underwood’s lifelong project.

Lot Essay:
In 1942, while stationed with the Pioneer Corps in Wiltshire, Keith Vaughan and his company were tasked with clearing the overgrown grounds of Greenways Preparatory School at Ashton Gifford House, a three-story Neo-Classical building in a hamlet of Codford. What seemed at first a monotonous military duty soon proved to be a profound source of artistic inspiration for Vaughan, leading to some of his most important wartime works, including The Working Party (1942), Tree Felling at Ashton Gifford (1942–43), and the present work, The Garden at Ashton Gifford (1944).

The work at Ashton Gifford revealed a striking balance between the physical demands of military labor. At times exhausting, it proved monotonous during others, thus allowing moments of quiet observation and creative energy. For Vaughan, such manual work became a study in rhythm and form. Soldiers, often assisted by local residents and schoolchildren, felled trees and dragged branches by hand, scenes that inspired the artist to capture the setting, as he wrote to his friend Norman Towne, “in lassoes of line and nets of color,” recording “white and ochre branches plunging into the oceanic surging of tangled nettles.”

Most of the works Vaughan produced at the time were rapid pen-and-ink or pencil sketches, reflecting his growing fascination with structure, gesture, and movement. In the late 1960s, he revisited several of these wartime studies, reworking them in gouache and wax pastel to soften the dense pen lines and bring new vitality to the compositions. Although early and colored, the present work already exemplifies this synthesis: the detailed figures in the foreground, rendered in ink, contrast with the pale, textured washes and touches of green pastel in the background, creating a measured balance between Vaughan’s Neo-Romantic expressiveness of the 1940s and the more restrained abstraction characteristic of his later style.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
This dynamic composition is a preparatory study for one of the eight full-page lithographs Henry Moore created to illustrate André Gide’s French translation of Goethe’s Prometheus, published by Henri Jonquières in Paris in 1951. Goethe’s Prometheus reimagines the ancient Titan who defied Zeus by bringing fire and knowledge to humankind, as a symbol of creative independence and human resilience. For Goethe, as for later Romantic artists, Prometheus embodied the self-reliant creator who draws power from his own imagination rather than divine authority.

The image derives from a page of studies once belonging to Moore’s Promethée sketchbook (Notebook 7, HMF 2564), which the artist later disassembled and sold in 1984. While the sketchbook is generally dated 1949–50, Moore did not receive the commission until December 1949, suggesting that most related drawings were executed in 1950. A related version, in darker tones, is held in a private American collection (HMF 2592).

The present composition illustrates the Death of Mira, a dramatic episode unique to Goethe’s version. In this scene, Prometheus’s daughter Pandora recounts her friend Mira’s descent into death, prompting her father’s lyrical reflection on mortality. Goethe’s verses describe death not as destruction but as transformation; an inward journey in which the self encompasses an entire world.

provenance:
We wish to thank Mrs. Julia Pechstein, Hamburg, for kindly confirming the authenticity of the present lot, which will be accompanied by a certificate of authenticity dated September 3, 2025.

Lot Essay:
A prolific painter and printmaker, Max Pechstein is perhaps best known as a German Expressionist painter of the Die Brücke group in the years before World War I. Along with Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Emil Nolde, they helped define a particular emotionally charged style of painting that looked to the French Fauves and primitivist art, using strong, vibrant color and angularity of lines and shapes. Pechstein spent most of the year 1908 in Paris where he experienced the work of the Fauves firsthand, including Henri Matisse and Paul Gauguin, later that year moving to Berlin and seeing Matisse's paintings again at Paul Cassirer Gallery.

In 1914, the artist and his wife, in search of inspiration from more primitive art forms, traveled to Palau, an island in the western Pacific Ocean, where they were captured and imprisoned in Japan at the start of the First World War. They were later sent back to Germany and Pechstein fought in the war, becoming a more radical Socialist politically as the war drew to a close. After his service, Pechstein returned to Berlin and held a professorship teaching art at the Berlin Academy, experiencing a burst of creative energy and revisiting his Expressionist style of painting.

In the years following his war service, the artist grappled with depression, especially during the long, cold German winters, and he sought refuge at a vacation home in the fishing village and artist colony of Nidden (Nida, Lithuania) on the Baltic Sea coast. In 1921, when Nidden ceased to belong to Germany under the Treaty of Versailles, the artist set about searching for a new enclave. Setting off alone in the spring of 1921, he travelled on foot along the coast until he discovered Leba (Pomerania, now Poland), a seaside resort town located on the Baltic coast near the Łebsko Lake. The artist was struck by the natural beauty of the village, where he settled and immediately found renewed artistic inspiration: "…the new landscapes, the new people, I gorged myself upon them," the artist wrote, "I have the farmland behind, a far broader subject than in Nidden" (Pechstein, quoted in A. Soika, Max Pechstein: Das Werkverzeichnis der Ölgemälde, Vol. I, 1905-1918, Munich, 2011, p. 73). It was in Leba, during highly productive summer stays, that the present watercolor was executed, along with the other two works in our sale: House with Field, 1922 (Lot 22) and Fishing Boats in the Lebastrom II, 1933 (Lot 25).

Created in the summer of 1931, Fishermen on the Gardnosee by Moonlight shows eel fisherman on Lake Gardno, a large lake to the southwest of Leba, with Mount Rowokół in the background. The lake once teemed with eels, which are nocturnal predators and as such, are typically caught at night, with a full moon causing a high tide further ensuring the fishermen’s success. Here, the artist has depicted with intensity and vigor a scene of striking complementary blue and yellow pigments flanked by verdant foliage. Albert Marquet first visited Algiers in the winter of 1920–21, beginning what would become a lasting and profound attachment to North Africa. Lot Essay:
French painter and printmaker Édouard Vuillard was an important member of Les Nabis, a group of Post-Impressionists influential at the end of the 19th-century. Born in 1868 in Cuiseaux, France, his family moved to Paris when he was ten. Vuillard’s father passed away when he was a teenager, leaving him with his mother and sister, Marie. Vuillard’s mother worked at home, running a dressmaking company to support the family. Vuillard lived with her until her death 45 years later. His family life greatly influenced his art, painting mostly women, especially his mother and sister, in domestic environments: a mundus muliebris as literature on Vuillard often describes.

Vuillard trained in Paris at various institutions including the Lycée Julian and the École des Beaux Arts, to which he was eventually admitted after three unsuccessful attempts to gain entrance. He traveled extensively around Europe before exhibiting at his first Salon des Independents in 1901, which signaled the launch of his career and those of Les Nabis painters. 

The Nabis drew inspiration from Edgar Degas and Paul Gauguin and leaned toward a flatter, more decorative rendering of space, betraying the laws of linear perspective and tonal modeling. The Nabis de-emphasized the descriptive value of color and form; suddenly, they were vehicles through which emotions and abstract ideas could be conveyed. The group was inspired by Japanese prints which similarly employed color, line, and pattern to create striking, bold compositions. They, too, favored playful aesthetics over naturalism.  

Profil de Marie à Contre-Jour (Profile of Marie Against the Light), however, is no mosaic of embellishment. A more streamlined composition, it depicts the silhouette of Vuillard’s sister, Marie, against an illuminating window. It is almost completely devoid of pattern despite a series of gray vertical lines in the background, perhaps a curtain. Otherwise, yellow light consumes most of the background, casting her profile in a dark shadow.  

Marie, who Vuillard affectionately referred to as Mimi, was known to be shy and quiet. If Vuillard’s Nabis instinct was to reflect an emotional or abstract truth through form and color, then perhaps Profil de Marie visually manifests Marie’s introversion. The shadow masks her face, anonymizing her. In contrast to the bright outdoors, she sits alone in a dark room, preferring the comfort and isolation of her home. Vuillard said “I don’t paint portraits. I paint people in their homes.” His paintings do not simply capture the likeness of his subjects but convey a more intimate and comprehensive understanding of their character. 

Profil de Marie maintains the decorative, experimental charm of Vuillard’s style. Here, Vuillard does not blend figure and setting in a mass of ornamentation but visually utilizes a continuous shadow. Marie's silhouette bleeds into the gray around her. In Vuillard’s work, the subject becomes a sort of extension of their environment: a mere decoration, possibly a broader comment on the expected domestic role of women in late nineteenth century France. 

Early on in his career, Vuillard designed theatrical sets, exercising his lifelong love for drama and literature. He often approached his paintings as if they were sets, carefully planning the composition with a narrative in mind: “what little there is must be thought out completely, forms and colors (the old idea of the intentional).” If Profil de Marie is a theatrical set, then Marie is a shadow puppet, at the will of the puppeteer: the artist himself.

With a distinctive use of bold outlines and vibrant colors, Fishing Boats in the Lebastrom II, 1933, recalls the Fauve painters, and exemplifies the formal explorations of Pechstein of the time. Under a pale sky, the boats and their reflections in the almost mirror-like water come alive with energetically applied streaks of color, and there is a marked contrast between the flatness of the picture plane and abundance of rich detail. The words of Max Osborn could have described Pechstein’s intention in this very watercolor: 'He wants to capture the pulsating brightness, the interweaving of the blinding light and the wonderful clear air, or the filtering effect that occurs through the humid atmospheric veil. The whole series of Leba pictures allows us to observe a new development. The colorful expression has kept its layered flatness, but it is richer, and more lively in its structure' (M. It is a testament to the artist’s continuous experimentation with the lexicon of Expressionism applied to a region, a culture, a season, an atmosphere, a feeling so profoundly beloved by the artist.

Lot Essay:
As a student, Rivera became well acquainted with European Post-Impressionist and Symbolist trends, largely through his professors Germán Gedovius and Julio Ruelas, who had studied in Munich and Karlsruhe. While firmly grounded in academic training, he was equally eager to explore contemporary movements and engaged actively with writers, poets, intellectuals, architects, and fellow artists of his generation. In this way, he embodied the spirit of his era, a product of Mexican Modernism at the close of the Porfirio Díaz regime (1907–1910). His first solo exhibition coincidentally opened during the Centennial Celebrations of Mexican Independence, marking a symbolic convergence of artistic and national transformation.

By 1905, Rivera sought to continue his studies in Europe. Though he initially lacked formal funding from the National School of Fine Arts, he eventually secured financial support from the Governor of Veracruz, Don Teodoro Dehesa, enabling him to sail to Spain in 1907. He later settled in Paris and traveled throughout Northern Europe, deepening his exposure to contemporary European art.

The present work dates from 1906, just before Rivera’s departure to Europe and the beginning of his broader artistic experimentation. By this time, he had already earned high praise from local critics and intellectuals, with poet José Juan Tablada lauding his mastery of charcoal. Although executed in Mexico, the work channels the art of European masters Rivera deeply admired, including Arnold Böcklin, Franz von Stuck, Pierre Puvis de Chavannes, James Ensor, and Jan Toorop. It shares aesthetic, formal, and technical affinities with Dead Horse (gouache and charcoal on paper, MoMA collection), also executed in 1906 and signed in the same manner. Both works reflect Rivera’s early ability to balance rigorous academic training with the innovative spirit of European modernism, which he was yet to fully encounter.

Lot Essay:
Illustrating a clear, bright day, possibly along the river Seine at Tournedos-sur-Seine in Normandy, Bords de Rivière, is a superb example of Gustave Loiseau’s gently diffusive light as it reflects off the flowing water. Considered one of the foremost post-impressionist painters, he was greatly influenced by the generation of impressionists who came before him, including Claude Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, and Camille Pissarro. Born in Paris to parents who ran a successful butcher shop, Loiseau was apprenticed to a house painter and then to a decorator, which aroused his interest in art. In 1887, he received an inheritance from his grandmother that allowed him to study art full time. He briefly attended the Ecole des Arts Décoratifs and then studied under the landscape painter Fernand Just Quignon.

On the advice of Quignon, in 1890, Loiseau traveled to Pont-Aven in Brittany, where he befriended the artists Maxime Maufra and Henry Moret. As he was mostly self-taught, Loiseau shaped his style through close observation of nature and careful scrutiny of his impressionist forebears. Like them, he was a champion of painting en plein air, yet he developed his own artistic technique that used a distinct cross-hatched brushstroke, called en treillis. This method created an evanescent quality and movement to his compositions and reveals the influence of pointillism in his work.
In 1895, Loiseau was introduced by Claude Monet to the art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, who signed an exclusive contract with him two years later. The resulting financial independence allowed the artist to journey throughout France to paint various landscapes, including Normandy, where Tournedos-sur-Seine is located, and Brittany, as well as the small towns along the rivers Seine and Yonne. By 1904, Loiseau settled in Pontoise, a suburb northwest of Paris. Located along the river Oise, the town was popularized by Pissarro, who was later followed by other artists who came to depict the waterfront views.

Analogous to Monet, Loiseau explored in his canvases the different atmospheric conditions of rivers and their surrounding landscapes, often from a variety of views that range from misty mornings to brilliant, sunshine filled afternoons, such as can be seen in the present artwork. The richly pigmented surface is composed of spontaneous brushwork that is layered to create a scintillating dance of light. Tall trees line the riverbanks and are cast with deep, purpled shadows. The water and grass that line the summer-bright path dazzle with staccato strokes of blue, green, yellow, and violet. Three small figures can be seen at the focal point of the composition. Their miniscule presence serves to accentuate the broad expanse of river and land under the sweeping blue sky. This work masterfully highlights Loiseau’s experimental nature and his intuitive use of both impressionist and post-impressionist techniques to capture nature as it is experienced.

Lot Essay:
Painted at the onset of World War One, the present work portrays the artist’s wife of fourteen years, Maria Van Rysselberghe. Née Maria Monnom, she occupied a central place in her husband’s artistic and intellectual life, introducing him to figures such as Émile and Marthe Verhaeren and to André Gide, of whom she would become a close confidante. The portrait conveys her assertive temperament, which captivated so many writers and artists of her time. It also represents a synthesis in Van Rysselberghe’s artistic development, uniting his disciplined concern for color and light rooted in Pointillism with a more introspective and emotionally responsive mode of portraiture. 

Although he had initially embraced Divisionism after encountering Georges Seurat and Paul Signac in 1886, and promoted the movement in Belgium through his involvement with the avant-garde group Les XX, Théo van Rysselberghe here abandons his signature precisionist approach. His brushwork becomes broader more fluid, and guided less by optical theory than by intuition, enriched by soft color harmonies that recall Whistler’s most tonal works. In Maria van Rysselberghe au Coin du Feu, the artist replaces the small, contrasting touches of pure color characteristic of his earlier work with nuanced modulations of hue and light that evoke both atmosphere and psychological depth. The diagonal placement of the sitter introduces a quiet sense of movement while preserving compositional poise. The painting’s visual equilibrium depends on the interplay of silvery highlights: Maria’s hair, her pale dress, the white mantelpiece subtly contrast against the enveloping warmth of reds and greens that define the interior.

Through this controlled orchestration of tone and structure, Van Rysselberghe transforms the analytic rigor of Neo-Impressionism into a deeply personal language of feeling, one that speaks to the affection and admiration he held for his wife.

Lot essay:
Beginning his training at the age of eleven, Rivera attended drawing lessons at the Old Academy of San Carlos [Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes], studying under some of the most renowned Mexican artists of the era such as Julio Ruelas, a distinguished Art Nouveau and Symbolist draughtsman, and the experienced Catalan Antonio Fabrés, who had recently become director of painting and implemented a new curriculum. 

Under Fabrés Rivera learned the scientific “Pillet Method,” developed by French artist Jules Jean Désiré Pillet, which emphasized real life observation over copying classical statues or lithographs. Between 1903 and 1906, Rivera produced early works that capture landscapes and everyday activities of ordinary people, as exemplified by the present work, which illustrates Rivera’s application of European trends to his own Mexican reality. This 1906 rural scene, executed shortly before his departure to Europe, exemplifies Rivera’s drawing method grounded in direct observation. Here, the artist depicts common Mexican life—peasants working the land and a woman grinding corn—a subject that would later become central to Rivera’s iconography after his return to Mexico in 1921, particularly within the Mexican Modern School and the frescoes of the Mural Movement.

By November 1906, Rivera participated in a celebrated group exhibition at the Escuela Nacional de Bellas Artes, presenting paintings, pastels, and watercolors. While only a few of these works were reviewed in contemporary newspapers and magazines, some have resurfaced over the past century, while others remain undiscovered. It is plausible that this drawing was among Rivera’s contributions to his final exhibition at his training school, executed under Fabrés’s innovative approach to drawing.

Lote Essay:
Painted in 1921, Paysage Français belongs to a pivotal phase in André Lhote’s career, when the artist sought to reconcile the structural rigor of Cubism with the harmony inherent to a classical composition. Having first embraced Cubism around 1910, Lhote gradually transformed its geometric discipline into a more lyrical and accessible language, as evidenced here. At the time of the completion of the present lot, the artist was pursuing a synthesis between modern form and traditional subject, applying Cubist principles to the French landscape with a distinctive sense of order and clarity.

Paysage Français depicts an expansive view of the bridge and village of Vic-sous-Thil in Burgundy, a motif Lhote revisited several times during this period. His characteristic use of interlocking planes and rhythmic diagonals transforms the rural scene into a dynamic architectural structure, animated by a palette of ochres and greens that both anchor the composition and evoke the influence of Paul Cézanne. Here, Lhote reaffirms the enduring vitality of nature reimagined through a Cubist lens, embodying his conviction that modern art should unite analysis and equilibrium rather than pursue abstraction for its own sake.

Lot Essay:
Claire Roy, wife of the French poet, novelist, and art critic Claude Roy, was a close friend and confidante of Françoise Gilot at the time of her relationship with Pablo Picasso, during the 1940s and early 1950s. Both couples moved within the same vibrant postwar Parisian intellectual circle that included writers, artists, and critics such as Paul Éluard, Jean-Paul Sartre, and Simone de Beauvoir. The Roys were also among Picasso and Gilot’s frequent visitors in the South of France, particularly in Vallauris and Golfe-Juan, where the couple settled in 1948.

In her celebrated autobiography My Life with Picasso (1964), Gilot refers to the Roys with warmth and affection, noting Claire’s intelligence and generosity of spirit. As reflected in the present work, Claire Roy was far more than a social acquaintance for Gilot: she served as a confidante and ally within an otherwise male-dominated milieu. Here, Gilot depicts herself portraying her friend, in a composition that recalls her contemporary double portraits with her "other" alter ego, Geneviève Alicquot, thus implying a quiet sorority between artist and model, and placing them on equal footing.

Literature:
Antoinette Le Normand-Romain, The Bronzes of Rodin, Catalogue of Works in the Musée Rodin, Éditions de la Réunion des Musées Nationaux, Paris, 2007, no. S.1578 (other versions illustrated pp. 168-169).

Lot Essay:
In July 1891, Rodin was commissioned by the Société des Gens de Lettres, then chaired by Émile Zola, to create a monument to the writer Honoré de Balzac. Deeply captivated by the project, Rodin embarked on exhaustive research, studying every known likeness of Balzac. Believing that regional physiognomy was essential to capturing the author’s essence, he traveled to Balzac’s native Touraine, where he discovered a local driver, Monsieur Estager, whose features closely resembled those of the writer. From Estager, Rodin made two masks that served as the foundation for his sculptural portrait.

Rodin’s fascination with Balzac went beyond mere physical likeness; he was drawn to the author’s monumental intellect, literary presence, and complex character. This intense study of Balzac’s personality and form informed Rodin’s groundbreaking approach, which sought to convey the writer’s inner vitality as much as his outward appearance.

The present work, executed in 1892, is one of Rodin’s earliest studies for the portrait and served as a precursor to his first full-figure model, the so-called ‘Nude study C’ which which shows shows a naked Balzac standing with folded arms and a protruding belly, a version before the dressed final bronze, which was ultimately rejected by the commissioning society.

Our bronze stops at the author's bust. The earliest but also smallest version, it was cast by the foundry Alexis Rudier for the dealer Gustave Danthon, who acquired the rights to reproduce all bronzes derived from the original plaster. After Rodin’s death, Danthon produced reductions of the face and several variants of the bust in 1918, as shown here. The Musée Rodin repurchased most of the plaster models and their reproduction rights in 1927 and 1933. At least three bronzes of this bust, Première version, Petit Modèle, are known to have been executed by Danthon.

provenance:
We wish to thank the Comité Giacometti for kindly confirming the authenticity of the present lot, which was examined in Paris in June, 2025. It is now recorded in the Alberto Giacometti Database under no. 4729.

Lot Essay:
In 1928, Alberto Giacometti was offered a one-year contract by the Parisian gallery owner, Pierre Loeb. Loeb was the preeminent dealer of the Surrealists, and this opportunity cemented the artist’s entrée to that circle, to whom he had previously been introduced to by André Masson. Giacometti was to remain a friend of Loeb, of whom he made several portraits in 1946, including the present work, as well as in 1949, to prepare an etching that was to illustrate a text written by Loeb on figurative art.

1946 was a pivotal year for Giacometti in his artistic development. In an essay accompanying the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum’s 1974 retrospective on the artist, Reinhold Hohl stated that it was this year that the artist, “…realized that space does not exist merely in front of a figure, but surrounds and separates it from other objects. When we look at something, we see as much of this space (particularly at the sides of the object) as our field of vision permits. The figure seen at a distance appears pronouncedly thin in relation to the absolute standard of our field of vision. As a consequence of its thinness, the figure also appears relatively tall. The change from the tiny representations of the preceding years to the elongated figures of 1946 resulted from new studies—mostly drawings—from nature.” (Alberto Giacometti: A Retrospective Exhibition, New York, 1974, p. 24)

Pierre Loeb Seated in the Office of the Galerie Pierre / Pierre Loeb Seated, 1946, reveals the artist’s experimentation of this time. The recto depicts the dealer in his Paris gallery, sitting in an armchair and smoking a pipe, while the verso presents several sketches of heads. Yet despite the unquestionable likeness, there is a degree of elusiveness to the sitter’s facial features and body, a certain “lack of precision” to his portrayal that highlights its, “forever changing,” fleeting nature (Paul Moorhouse, Giacometti: Pure Presence, London, 2015, p. 150). The real subject matter of the artwork is “…space, this three-dimensional matter which has neither substance nor color, which is a sharply felt presence, but can only be negatively located between and around the objects which obstruct it.” (Alberto Giacometti, 1974, p. 35) The short lines used to compose this space accumulate to form a web between crossing objects, and may stand for the trace of the artist’s eye, “…swiftly and incessantly moving around the composition from one object to another, measuring the distances between them.” (Ibid., p. 35)

As Moorhouse notes with regards to the artist’s portraiture, “To an extreme degree, Giacometti’s art lays bare the complexities and ambiguities of perception, relentlessly exposing the fugitive and elusive nature of visual experience. His portraits are in that sense not simply depictions of individuals. Rather, they are sights that bear evidence of the artist’s struggle to comprehend and express an unfathomable human presence.” (Moorhouse, p. 15). A related drawing from the same year, with Loeb in a similar posture and setting, is held by the Centre Pompidou, Paris. It is drawings such as these that led Giacometti to his post-War sculptural style, which consequently may be characterized as drawing in space.

Literature:

Lot Essay:
Still life occupied a central place in Bernard Buffet’s œuvre from the very beginning of his career. Throughout the 1950s, he returned to the genre repeatedly, firmly asserting his commitment to figuration over abstraction while also channeling a centuries-old tradition inherited from the Old Masters.

In a deceptively simple interior, mundane-yet-highly-symbolic objects (such as a few coins, a petrol lamp, a toppled empty wine glass, as well as a large titular checkerboard) are arranged on a plain round table. Without a doubt, Le Jacquet reads as a modern vanitas, inspired by the French 17th century still lifes Buffet so admired at the Louvre. Stripped of anecdotal detail, each object is rendered with a gravity and monumentality that lend it an almost architectural presence, every form delineated by Buffet’s unmistakable black contours. The emphasis on sharp outlines, the restrained palette of greys and browns, and the use of humble objects became hallmarks of Buffet’s distinctive style in the 1950s. In the present work, such signature features heighten the austere mood and evoke a profound sense of solitude, echoing the existentialist writings of Albert Camus and Jean-Paul Sartre, to whose cultural milieu Buffet’s work is often linked.

Far from a decorative exercise, Le Jacquet stands as a visual reflection of post-war trauma and Buffet’s personal meditation on time, fragility, and isolation — an obsession seemingly rooted in the artist's own life. Pierre Bergé, Buffet's lover at the time, understood the biographical vein of Buffet’s paintings particularly his still lifes, pointing out: “Buffet is present everywhere in his paintings [...] This is particularly true for Buffet. He looks like his paintings.”

provenance:
We wish to thank Mr. Romain Lefebfre for kindly confirming the authenticity of the present lot on the basis of digital photographs, which will be included in his forthcoming Catalogue Raisonné of the artist's work.

Lot Essay:
This muscular study relates to Jean Dupas’s grand decorative cycle La Gloire de Bordeaux, painted in 1937 for the apse of the conference hall at the Bourse du Travail in Bordeaux. The monumental composition, still in situ today, celebrates the city’s vitality and prosperity through allegorical figures representing the river Garonne, and various Olympic gods such as Neptune, Bacchus and Ceres, as well as several Muses of the Arts, all surrounding the city’s coat of arms.

Likely depicting the Allegory of Tragedy, as a nod to the city’s important contribution to French theater, the present drawing exemplifies Dupas’s refined synthesis of classical tradition and modern form. A leading exponent of modern classicism, Dupas here combines the precision of an Ingresque line with elongated proportions, a subtle cubist stylization through the mastery use of charcoal, which is characteristic of his mature style. The figure’s sculptural modeling and sensual contours only reveal his exceptional draughtsmanship, which shouldn’t come as a surprise for an artist who won the famous Grand Prix de Rome in 1910, allowing him to study the work of many Renaissance masters, especially Michelangelo, in Rome. 

Dupas achieved national and international renown through major decorative commissions, from the Tour des Vins de France at the 1925 Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs to the celebrated Art Deco interiors of the ocean liner Normandie. With the Bourse du Travail project—commissioned by Bordeaux’s visionary mayor Adrien Marquet—Dupas affirmed both his artistic stature and the civic ambition of a city eager to combine beauty with progress.

Lot Essay:
In October 1940, fleeing the war in Europe, Fernand Léger settled in New York, a city he had first visited in 1931 and where he remained until the end of the global conflict in 1945.

Léger’s American years proved exceptionally productive. When he returned to France in December 1945, he is said to have shipped back five crates containing some fifty-seven paintings and more than one hundred twenty drawings and studies. Although he remained closely connected to French expatriate circles and resisted full assimilation into American life, Léger was deeply impressed by the country’s energy and industrial vigor. Reflecting near the end of his stay, he observed: “In America you are confronted with power in motion, with force in reserve without end. An unbelievable vitality — a perpetual movement. One has the impression that there is too much of everything.” (Interview with André Warnod, Arts[Paris], January 4, 1946, pp. 1–2; quoted in Simon Willmoth, Léger and America, exh. cat., London and Stuttgart, 1987–88, p. 43).

The present work, executed in 1942, is a design for the cover of Fortune, the magazine founded by Henry Luce, which sought to be “the most beautiful” in American publishing through its collaboration with leading modern artists and photographers such as Diego Rivera, Ben Shahn, Ralston Crawford, Ansel Adams, Walker Evans, and Edward Steichen. Although this design was never published (unlike the cover Léger completed for Fortune the previous year), it marked a renewed engagement with graphic design, a field he had enthusiastically explored after the First World War but largely set aside between 1923 and 1947. The composition reveals how American visual culture reinvigorated his formal vocabulary: against sweeping rays of yellow, red, and blue—colors central to his modernist palette—Léger orchestrates a striking interplay of monumental oil derricks, industrial frameworks, and the colossal head of a man whose direct gaze confronts the viewer. The figure’s stoic presence becomes a silent emblem of humanity’s confrontation with the mounting global tensions of the early 1940s.

In 1950, at age 73, Raoul Dufy traveled to Boston for treatment of severe arthritis in his hands. Undaunted by his condition, the artist continued to paint, and created numerous watercolors of America from New England to Arizona during his sojourn. Upon the invitation of Life magazine, Dufy also visited New York City, where he depicted baseball games, the Brooklyn Bridge, and Trinity Church, among other scenes, all of which convey the lively energy of the city.

Many of the works he made while in New York were featured in the January 22, 1951 issue of Life, including the present work. The caption that accompanies the illustration of New York Billboards, 1950, is indicative of Dufy's ebullient view of the world: "Time's Square," thought the artist, 'was spectacular like a ballet.' 'Ah, le Kleenex' he murmured..." The bold and bright billboards of Times Square are a perfect vehicle for the French artist's vivid colors and expressive, rapid brushstrokes, which permitted him to capture the spontaneity and movement of the beating heart of the city that never sleeps. It is a fitting subject for a painter of modern life whose art unabashedly relished in joy and pleasure.

Lot Note:
The present bronze, with no known record of public exhibition during the artist’s lifetime, exemplifies Rodin’s fascination with mythological water creatures as a means of exploring movement, sensuality, and the expressive potential of the human body. As the critic Caille Mauclair observed, Rodin’s small groups, such as this one, sought “new combinations of movement to make a dynamic art."

While respecting traditional representations of a tailed triton and a winged siren, Rodin here does not reference any specific mythological episode. The interaction between the figures is formal rather than narrative, emphasizing fleeting gestures rather than lasting contact. Without relying on classical sources, he captures fluid, undulating poses that evoke the motion of water itself. Rodin famously favored twisting forms, visible here in the male torso and thighs, which coil around the siren while leaving sensual space between them, compelling the viewer to engage with the group from multiple angles. “The couple’s energy,” Mauclair notes, “lies in the fact that no parts of their bodies move in the same direction or lie in a common plane,” highlighting Rodin’s mastery of dynamic, multidirectional motion.

Lot essay:
Largely a self-taught artist, Kees van Dongen grew up in Rotterdam, in the Netherlands, and was famously expelled from school as a child for constantly sketching in class. The artist became a keen observer of the landscape and people around him, painting the surrounding countryside and the dock workers nearby as he honed his skills. He made a small living drawing for newspapers and magazines, both to accompany news stories and satirically. After a day trip to Paris in 1897, van Dongen fell in love with the city and moved there permanently, living at the Bateau-Lavoir in Montmartre with fellow Fauve artists. His portrait studies began at this time, and he frequently enlisted Montmartre prostitutes as his models, as he did not have money to pay more professional models.

While van Dongen was steeped in the avant-garde art world of turn-of-the-century Paris, he quite naturally gravitated toward a Fauvist style independently, always experimenting with bold, bright colors and compositions bordering on abstraction. In the 1910s, his mistress Léa Alvin (also known as Jasmy Jacob), a fashion director and socialite, greatly influenced his style and also introduced him to the upper class and aristocratic society of Paris. Soon, having one’s portrait painted by van Dongen became so fashionable and desirable, his list of sitters came to include Josephine Baker, Brigitte Bardot, Maurice Chevalier, Anatole France, Fernande Olivier and King Leopold III. Of painting the portraits of high society women in particular, the artist once quipped: "The essential thing is to elongate the women and especially to make them slim. After that it just remains to enlarge their jewels. They are ravished."

While the exact identity of the present painting’s sitter, Dora, is not known, she appears to be one of the socialites the artist was frequently commissioned to paint. Unlike most of his other portraits, though, Dora is not adorned with the jewels and lavish clothing common to van Dongen’s social circles. This allowed the artist to play with color directly on her skin, the green shadow falling across her shoulder, and her captivating hazel-blue eyes and blushing cheeks recalling the artist’s Fauvist origins.

Lot Essay:
Painted in 1958, La Tour Eiffel stands as one of Bernard Buffet’s most striking homages to the French capital — a city where he was born and which he never ceased to depict throughout his long and prolific career.

Specifically, this work belongs to a cycle of Parisian views known as Paysages de Paris, initiated in 1956 and exhibited at Galerie David et Garnier. Comprised of about twenty paintings, the series featured landmarks such as Notre-Dame, the Sacré-Cœur, Tour Saint-Jacques, and the Eiffel Tower as depicted here. Its success was such that Buffet soon expanded the project to other metropolises, including London and New York, confirming his ability to invest urban landmarks with profound psychological depth, and to transform them into emblems of both personal and collective identity. 

In this canvas, the Eiffel Tower ascends with stark monumentality from a dense layering of Haussmannian roofs and chimneys, their angular contours delineated in Buffet’s signature black lines. With its somber, monochrome palette of grey-blues and earthy browns, La Tour Eiffel evokes the biting cold of Parisian winters and the atmosphere of a society still haunted by the shadow of the Second World War. The result is at once a portrait of the city and a reflection of the post-war condition: an austere, expressionist realism that captures beauty inseparable from melancholy. Rising above this urban mass, the tower thus becomes more than a landmark: it is transfigured into a symbol of modernity, a stark emblem of the city’s endurance.

It also acts as Buffet’s double in that it embodies all the hopes and expectations placed in Buffet’s persona, then considered the only artist able to save non-abstract Modern painting in Post-War France. By 1958, Buffet had indeed already consolidated his reputation as one of the leading painters of his generation, having won the Prix de la Critique at only 20 years old, being awarded first prize by Connaissance des Arts in 1955, and becoming the subject of a retrospective at Galerie Charpentier the same year this present work was executed.

Lot Essay:
“It is quite simple: my drawings are the key to my work… I have drawn all my life; I started my life drawing,” declared Auguste Rodin ahead of his 1910 Paris exhibition (Les Dessins d’Auguste Rodin, cited in Judrin, Osterwold et al., Auguste Rodin: Aquarelles de la Collection du Musée Rodin, 2004, p. 9), underscoring the central role of drawing in his practice.

As he explained to the writer Antony Ludovici around 1900, drawing served as a means to “test” the connection between eye and hand—an instinctive process through which he internalized “the subtle secrets of the human form” (Personal Reminiscences of Auguste Rodin, 1926, pp. 138–9; cited in Elsen and Varnedoe, The Drawings of Rodin, 1972, pp. 85, 118). Less concerned with likeness, Rodin sought instead to capture motion and vitality. As journalist Mario Meunier observed in 1914, Rodin would draw without glancing at the paper, tracing the model’s movements in uninterrupted gestures before discarding the sheets to the floor—later reviewing, tracing, and occasionally coloring them (Les Marges, April 1914, pp. 250–1; cited in Judrin, Osterwold et al., p. 17).

The present drawing epitomizes Rodin’s shift from the dense, romantic style of the 1880s to a freer, more spontaneous approach. The contours are thin and fluid; the heavy brown washes give way to light, flesh-toned watercolor. Executed swiftly, often in a single continuous line against a blank sheet, the work achieves a clarity of form while preserving the immediacy and vitality of movement.
